This tutorial starts with an existing study directory and an existing dataset.
It sets the study up with `hvtiR::setup()`, then takes it through data
registration, descriptive tables and EDA plots. A later tutorial can then begin
with a specific analysis type instead of repeating this setup.

[Start here](https://ehrlinger.github.io/hvtiR/articles/start-here.html) is the family's
getting-started page and explains `setup()` in full. This tutorial gives the call
for a study that already exists.

Adoption keeps the study's folder names and does not rename the legacy working
directories. It does delete files, including any file named `tp.*`, even one you
edited, so read [what adoption deletes](#what-adoption-deletes) before you run it.

If the study does not exist yet and you are starting from a newly delivered
dataset, follow [Start a new study](new-study.html) instead.

The executable example uses one 40-row synthetic dataset. Its files stay in a
temporary directory and disappear after the article renders. For translating
existing SAS descriptive jobs, see
[From SAS descriptive jobs to R](sas-to-r-descriptive.html).

## Set up the study

### Select the R version

If the study already has an `renv.lock`, its `R` `Version` entry records the R
version to preserve. Select that version in RStudio and restart the session.
Do not silently upgrade an already pinned study. If the study is not pinned,
select **R 4.6** instead of the older 4.4.1 default, restart the session and
confirm the active version:

```r
R.version.string
```

### Run `hvtiR::setup()`

Close any open project first (**File > Close Project**), so that R starts outside
the study. `setup()` replaces packages in the study's library, and a session
inside the project has those packages loaded. That is why the call names the
directory with `root`.

#### What adoption deletes {#what-adoption-deletes}

Adopting deletes three kinds of file anywhere in the study, and makes no backup:

- every file whose name starts with `tp.`, **matched by name alone**, so an edited
  or study-specific `tp.*` file goes too;
- every `binder.summaries.doc`;
- every other file whose name and exact content match one in the template corpus.

Before you run it, look through the study for `tp.*` files that hold work of your
own, and rename or copy any you need. To adopt without deleting anything, add
`cleanup = FALSE` to the call.

#### The call

```r
install.packages("pak")  # once per machine
pak::pak("ehrlinger/hvtiR")

hvtiR::setup(
  study = "EDIT: the Study Tracker title",
  study_tracker_id = 0L,  # EDIT: the Study Tracker ID
  root = "EDIT: the study directory",
  adopt = TRUE,
  identity_source = "manual"
)
```

An existing directory needs `adopt = TRUE`, even an empty one, or `setup()`
stops. A study in revision needs `upgrade = FALSE` as well, so that the versions
its lockfile pins cannot move.

`identity_source = "manual"` records that you typed the title and ID, so a new
`_study.yml` is marked unverified rather than checked against Study Tracker. A
`_study.yml` the study already has is not rewritten, and keeps its recorded source.

`setup()` writes `_study.yml` and a project file when one is missing, declares
the family and the standard analysis packages in the study's `DESCRIPTION`,
installs them into the study's own library and records them in `renv.lock`, then
restarts RStudio inside the project. If it stops partway, fix what it names and
run the same command again.

Do not run `renv::init()` or `organize_templates.sh` on the study: `setup()`
replaces both, and `renv::init()` starts the library over.

```{r}
#| label: synthetic-setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(hvtiRutilities)
library(hvtiRtemplates)
workspace <- withr::local_tempdir(.local_envir = environment())
adopted_root <- file.path(workspace, "legacy-study")
folders <- c("datasets", "descriptive", "distributions", "analyses",
             "graphs", "documents", "estimates")
dir.create(adopted_root)
for (folder in folders) dir.create(file.path(adopted_root, folder))
i <- seq_len(40L)
built <- data.frame(
  ccfid = i,
  dead = i %% 2L,
  iv_dead = i / 10,
  iv_fup = i / 10 + 1,
  year = 2000L + i %% 10L,
  female = i %% 2L,
  race_grp = 1L + i %% 3L,
  repair = as.integer(i %% 3L == 0L),
  age = 40 + i,
  bmi = 20 + i / 10,
  hx_chf = as.integer(i %% 4L == 0L),
  lvmassi = 80 + i,
  iv_opyrs = i + 0.25
)
utils::write.csv(
  built, file.path(adopted_root, "datasets", "built.csv"), row.names = FALSE
)
```

## Open the study as an RStudio Project

From here on, open the study's `.Rproj` whenever you work on it. RStudio starts
the session in the project directory, so there is no working-directory step to
remember or repeat, and `study_root()`, `open_job()` and `render_job()` find
`_study.yml` from anywhere inside the project.

Ask the study what it still needs, then attach the two packages used throughout
this tutorial:

```r
library(hvtiRutilities)
library(hvtiRtemplates)

normalizePath(".")
study_root()
study_status()
hvtiR::status()
```

Expect `study_status()` to report that no dataset is registered yet. That is the
next step.

When the Console is already at the study root, use `"."` anywhere a function
asks for `root`. The executable example below uses an explicit temporary path
only because it cannot open an RStudio Project while pkgdown renders the page.

The executable example needs no package environment, so it calls
`study_setup()`, the step of `setup()` that writes the study's identity, in its
temporary directory:

```{r}
#| label: adopt-study
# A vignette builds a throwaway study; in a real study, run hvtiR::setup().
study_setup(
  adopted_root,
  study = "Synthetic legacy study",
  study_tracker_id = 42L,
  adopt = TRUE,
  cleanup = FALSE,
  renv = FALSE
)
root <- adopted_root
```

## Add a package the study needs

`setup()` has already pinned the package environment. When a study needs a
package the family and the standard set do not bring, add it from inside the
project. That installs it, declares it and records it in `renv.lock`:

```r
hvtiRutilities::study_need("cmprsk")
```

## Register the existing dataset

Registration records the input filename, checksum and population. It does not
declare a study-wide endpoint or cohort: an endpoint-free descriptive job and
an event-time analysis can read the same dataset with different valid job
definitions.

```r
register_data(
  built = "built.csv",
  role = "study",
  population = "Patients meeting the study inclusion criteria"
)
verify_manifest()
```

Do not invent an outcome or follow-up field during setup. Each analysis job
declares its own outcome variables, coding, filters and cohort checks. The
descriptive jobs below depend only on a registered study dataset.

```{r}
#| label: register-data
register_data(
  adopted_root,
  built = "built.csv",
  role = "study",
  population = "Synthetic full cohort"
)
verify_manifest(file.path(adopted_root, "manifest.yaml"))
cfg <- study_config(adopted_root)
study_data <- read_built(cfg)
nrow(study_data)
```

Compare the registered file and its manifest checksum with the data build
before proceeding. A job that filters this data, or analyses an event and
follow-up time, must derive and check its own reference counts.

### If EDA uses a subset

The jobs can read the registered study dataset directly. If EDA needs a
subset, create it with a stated rule, save it as a separate dataset and
register that file too. For example:

```r
study_data <- read_built(study_config())
eda <- subset(study_data, age >= 50)  # Replace with the study's actual rule.
utils::write.csv(
  eda, file.path(study_dir("datasets"), "eda.csv"), row.names = FALSE
)
register_data(
  built = "eda.csv",
  dataset = "eda",
  role = "named",
  kind = "subset",
  population = "Patients age 50 or older"
)
```

In a job that uses this subset, set `DATASET <- "eda"` and
`ANALYSIS_SET <- NULL`. When the whole registered study dataset is the intended
population, use `DATASET <- "built"` and `ANALYSIS_SET <- NULL` instead. For a
subset of the study dataset that several jobs share, an analysis set is the
alternative: write it with `hvtiRdatabuild::write_analysis_set()` and read it
with `DATASET <- "built"` and the set's name in `ANALYSIS_SET`.

## Create the descriptive and EDA jobs

`open_job()` creates a missing job and opens it in RStudio. If the job already
exists, it opens the study-authored file without replacing any edits.

### Understand the name

Each call supplies four fields. `prefix` and `qualifier` select a template;
the other two fields keep related outputs together:

- `dc` means descriptive: the checks, tables and EDA plots. Legacy studies
  also hold `dp` (descriptive plot) jobs, which these templates replace.
- Qualifiers such as `general`, `tables` and `eda` select one template in
  that family.
- During EDA there may be no modeled endpoint or analysis method. `cohort`
  names the subject being described and `eda` names the stage. These are
  organizational labels, not invented analysis choices.

For example, `open_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", qualifier = "tables")`
creates `descriptive/dc.tables.cohort.eda.qmd` in an adopted legacy study.
Its HTML report stays beside the QMD, while its Word table goes under
`documents/cohort-eda/`. The trends and EDA report jobs sit in `descriptive/`
too, and their plot PNGs go under `graphs/cohort-eda/`.

### Start with the generally applicable jobs

Create general checks and descriptive tables for every registered study:

```r
general <- open_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", qualifier = "general")
tables <- open_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", qualifier = "tables")
```

The EDA report template is also part of this stage, but it requires a
meaningful `X_VAR` for the horizontal axis. Create it when the dataset has an
appropriate reference date, calendar year or follow-up measure:

```r
eda <- open_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", qualifier = "eda")
```

Its follow-up section needs the death and follow-up fields; take `"followup"`
out of `SECTIONS` when the data do not have them; `SECTIONS <- c("continuous",
"percent", "count")` draws the variable sections alone.

Two additional jobs are conditional. Add `dc-gfup` only when the registered
event and follow-up fields answer a real completeness question. Add `dc-trends`
only when the data have a meaningful calendar or operation-time field:

```r
gfup <- open_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", qualifier = "gfup")
trends <- open_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", qualifier = "trends")
```

The synthetic data have all of those fields, so the executable example
scaffolds all five jobs without opening editor windows:

```{r}
#| label: scaffold-example-jobs
study_jobs <- c(
  general = add_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", adopted_root, "general"),
  tables = add_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", adopted_root, "tables"),
  gfup = add_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", adopted_root, "gfup"),
  trends = add_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", adopted_root, "trends"),
  eda = add_job("dc", "cohort", "eda", adopted_root, "eda")
)
study_jobs
```

## Work the jobs and generate output

Each new job contains `EDIT:` markers for decisions that cannot come from the
template: variables, labels, groups, units and output choices. `open_job()`
opens the QMD in RStudio's file editor. Edit the file there, working from the
top marker downward, and **Render** to see what your choices do. A draft render
carries a DRAFT banner while any marker remains.

Always render; do not run the chunks by hand with **Run All**. Rendering starts
at the top in a clean session, much like running a SAS job from beginning to
end, so the report comes from this job alone. Run All works in your current
session, where an object or a setting left by another job can stand in for one
this job does not make. Render every edited job before leaving the study so the
saved QMD is still in an executable state. If you want the same final check from the Console, run
`render_job(tables, final = TRUE)`, substituting the job you edited.

The HTML report stays beside its QMD in `descriptive/`. The
descriptive Word table is filed under `documents/cohort-eda/`; trend and
EDA PNGs are filed under `graphs/cohort-eda/`. Open those artifacts and
check the population, variables, labels, counts, summaries and axes—not merely
that the files exist.

If the study has older SAS jobs, continue with
[From SAS descriptive jobs to R](sas-to-r-descriptive.html). That article owns
the detailed source mapping and migration workflow so adoption itself remains
short.

### When registered data change

Registration is endpoint-neutral: it records the dataset file, its population
description and manifest facts, but does not declare a study-wide endpoint or
cohort. After the study dataset is rebuilt, review the rebuilt file before
registering it. `hvtiRutilities::review_built()` compares the working file in
the datasets folder with its registered version and describes how the data
changed, without writing anything. It does not certify that the new file is
analytically or clinically correct; that judgment stays with you. When the
review reads as expected, `hvtiRutilities::update_manifest(dataset = "study")`
registers the rebuilt file as the next dated version, keeps every earlier
version and records the change in `manifest.yaml`. Jobs read the new version
from then on, so review dependent analysis sets and rerender their jobs.
